description: Arsman is a compound name formed from Ar (Fire) and Asman (Sky), symbolising a Fire in the Sky. Through this name, we represent our team as a spark of innovation and creativity, bringing our ideas to life as we take on this challenge.
summary:
Baramger (Kurdish for "Mars browser") is a web app that helps two astronauts plan a walk on Mars, stay safe, and do real science at each stop. It answers the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge by turning NASA data into one offline map of two walk zones in Jezero crater, where Perseverance works: Bright Angel (the "leopard spots" rock, Cheyava Falls) and Three Forks (the sample tube depot).

The app finds the safest route on a 2 m grid of real HiRISE terrain, never crosses ground steeper than 25°, checks the radio link to the habitat, and checks time, daylight, weather, sun storms and the load each astronaut carries. The crew can rehearse the walk in 3D, follow it on a tablet map or a helmet view, then replay it and get a report ready for Earth, with the light delay shown.

All maps, measurements and photos come from NASA, USGS and NOAA. Our slope map agrees with Perseverance's tilt sensor within 1.9° on average. This matters because the first people on Mars will walk where help from Earth is 3 to 22 minutes away: they need a map made for walkers, not only for scientists in orbit.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Baramger is a mission planner for a walk on Mars. It covers the whole walk:

- Plan (the evening before): choose the stops, find the safest route, and go through a safety list (time and reserve, steepest ground, radio contact with the habitat, daylight, sun activity, carried load, the buddy rule, turn-back times).

- Rehearse: fly along the route in 3D with the astronauts at real size (NASA's Z2 spacesuit model). Follow any astronaut.

- Walk: a tablet map and a helmet view guide the crew: the next stop, distance, time left, and warnings such as "sand ripples ahead".

- Report: replay the walk, compare the plan with what happened, and prepare a report for Earth with the real Earth–Mars light delay (11 minutes at the Earth–Mars distance of 15 November 2026).

- Ask: an AI assistant explains the plan in plain words. It may only use the mission data, and every answer is labelled "AI explanation" with its sources. It never decides what is safe: the app's own checks do.

Two walk zones are ready in Jezero crater: Z2 Bright Angel (around the Cheyava Falls "leopard spots" rock) and Z1 Three Forks (the depot where Perseverance left 10 sample tubes).

HOW IT WORKS

1. A Python data pipeline builds one offline "mission package" per walk zone: terrain grids, a 2 m routing grid with slope and roughness, no-go areas (steeper than 25°), rock types, map tiles, rover photos and positions, weather, daylight and sun activity. Every download is recorded with its address and time, and the package is checked against a schema that refuses a package without all five challenge resources.

2. The web app (TypeScript + CesiumJS) loads the package and does the rest in the browser: route search (A* with walking speed by slope, Tobler's hiking function), radio line of sight from the habitat antenna, safety checks, the walk, the replay and the report. Planning works without internet.

NASA DATA AT THE CORE

- JPL Mars Trek: HiRISE 25 cm photos and 1 m terrain (routes and slopes), CTX, THEMIS, MOLA and the Viking colour mosaic.

- USGS–NASA geologic map of Jezero crater (SIM 3464): the rock type at each stop and the official place names.

- Perseverance raw images and rover positions: what the crew will see at each stop.

- Perseverance MEDA weather (NASA PDS): real air and ground temperatures and air pressure.

- NASA DONKI: the number of solar particle events in the 30 days before each build (the flare and particle levels on screen come from NOAA SWPC).

- NASA's Z2 Spacesuit 3D model: the crew figures.

- Curiosity's route map (PIA23179) and NASA Worldview shaped the design (annotated route, layer list). Worldview is Earth data and is not used as Mars data.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

- Slope map vs Perseverance's own tilt sensor: 1.9° average difference at 79 rover positions (zone Z2), 1.3° at 124 positions (zone Z1).

- Sunrise and sunset (NASA GISS Mars24 equations): within 0.6 minutes of the times on NASA's Perseverance weather page.

- Earth–Mars signal delay (JPL approximate planet positions): checked against astropy to 0.0001 AU.

- Values that are not measured (for example walking speed, maximum slope, carried load) are called starting values, listed on screen, and marked "to verify".

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Crews and mission planners see the risks before the hatch opens: slopes, radio, time, weather and load on one screen.

- Scientists get more time at the rocks that matter.

- Students and the public can explore real places where Perseverance works, in any browser, with no login and nothing to install.

- Next steps: Moon walks for Artemis, live suit data (air, heart rate), tests with field crews on Earth, and more Mars zones from the same pipeline.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It joins orbit maps, rover photos and rover weather into one "walk view" for people on foot, from the whole planet down to the next step. The same data drives the plan, the 3D rehearsal, the helmet view and the replay. It tells the truth about its limits: approximate colours are labelled, the sky in the helmet view is labelled a drawing, and every photo carries its credit.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, Vite and CesiumJS (web app); Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy, rasterio/GDAL, Shapely, pyproj and Pillow (data pipeline); Vitest and pytest (tests); Vercel (live site); Cloudflare Workers (mission assistant API); GitHub Actions (tests on every change). Demo slides: pptxgenjs and qrcode (MIT), Microsoft PowerPoint, fonts Georgia and Franklin Gothic Book; the PDF is hosted on Google Drive.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Safety first (the AI never decides what is safe), honest data (no made-up values shown as measured), offline use (no internet on Mars), clear labels for anything approximate, data credits, and data rules: every extra source had to be official, documented, measured and free to use, with no link to China.

USE OF AI

We built Baramger with Claude Code, an AI coding assistant by Anthropic. It wrote most of the code, the documents and the demo slides, following our requests, and it checked data sources against our rules. The team chose the challenge and the idea and made the project's decisions: the place, the two walk zones, what to build, which data to allow, and the data rules. No AI image or video generator was used: the screenshots are of the real app, and the photos are NASA's except one credited leopard photo (Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0). Drawings made with AI in our documents carry a "Made with AI" mark; code made with AI is marked in its commit metadata. The app's Ask tab uses AI models (Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, Mistral, Cerebras) and labels every answer as AI.

Code, data packages and full credits: https://github.com/XAlandK/baramger

NASA does not endorse this project.
